articles.title: Why We’re Banning AI
articles.text:
We urgently need to protect human thought and creativity. Our magazine is committing itself to remaining handmade. Ensure every publication you support does the same.

Iam proud to say that as part of our new union contract, Current Affairs recently adopted one of the strictest anti-AI policies in the publishing industry. No text that is AI-generated may be published in our magazine. No AI-generated art may be used as a Current Affairs illustration. When you read Current Affairs, you are going to be reading the thoughts of a human, and seeing the results of human artistry.
We’re adopting this policy because we want to directly challenge the slopification of media. Newsrooms across the country are rushing to embrace AI and replace actual writers, public opinion be damned. The CEO of Business Insider, for instance, has said his publication is “all in on AI” (which is becoming an annoyingly common slogan) and shamelessly publishes AI-written content. At least they’re honest about it. Some publications have deliberately tricked people; Sports Illustrated was caught publishing AI-written pieces by nonexistent journalists. Guest op-eds in all of the major newspapers have been found to be either partly or wholly written by AI. Sometimes publishing this work can happen inadvertently; here at Current Affairs, we have had plenty of freelance submissions that use suspicious numbers of em-dashes and “this is not an X, it’s a Y” sentences. (We can’t promise that nothing will ever slip through the cracks, but we’re vigilant!) Astonishingly, though, some editors have actually defended publishing the pieces even when writers have been caught. The Wall Street Journal published an op-ed from a hedge fund billionaire, Stan Druckenmiller, that turned out to have been AI-generated (probably because billionaires are inarticulate due to a lifetime of never having to craft arguments to persuade the yes-men around them), but the paper defended publishing the piece, since it reflected the billionaire’s genuine opinion.
The trends are dire. But it’s obvious why these publications are rushing to replace writers. They are for-profit corporations, whose ultimate loyalty is to shareholders, not workers. AI is great for them, because it can produce “content” at a fraction of the expense that a writer costs. In fact, on the Milton Friedman theory that the only responsibility a business has is to increase its profits, CEOs are obligated to replace writers with AI if doing so is better for the bottom line. It’s a simple calculation: if producing 100 posts with AI costs almost nothing and takes four minutes, but paying a writer to produce 20 posts costs $5,000, well, why would you pay the writer? The calculation might hold even if the quality drops substantially, errors are introduced, and audience loyalty plummets. Even if you lost 60 percent of your readership, you might still make a lot more per story, because you can pump them out in seconds.
Futurism reports that despite the common narrative that AI has not led to major job loss, creative industries are being “eviscerated” by AI, which is fueling “one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history,” with more than 200,000 jobs in creative industries being lost in four years. The situation is horrible for artists. Game studios are now designing their worlds and levels using “art assets generated with full AI workflows.” As Brian Merchant reported earlier this year:

Opportunities and pay rates declining as clients and employers embrace generative AI. Artists getting more touch-up jobs and fewer well-paying, sustainable gigs. Pessimism, anger, and even despair, growing common, if not universal, in the field.

This is especially galling given that all of the AI models that are being used to replace artists were trained through the mass theft of those very same artists’ work!
Now here at Current Affairs, we’ve decided to say: fuck that! Over 62 beautiful print issues, we have commissioned hundreds of original, handmade artworks from brilliant artists around the world. We’ve published meticulously researched and edited articles, which often take weeks or months to go from the draft stage to publication. We spend ages working on our page layouts, poring over photographs for the magazine, tweaking sketches, moving sentences around in articles. The labor that goes into this magazine has been extensive from the start, and most of it is hidden from view. We do it because we care about quality. If you pick up a copy of our magazine, you’ll see the result. I think it’s clear when you read it that we actually care about what we’re putting out. It’s not just Content designed to farm clicks.

Current Affairs has always been a bit of an anachronism. We started a print magazine in 2016. Nobody thought this was a good idea. (The editor in chief of Vanity Fair told me to my face that this was a wholly misguided project and certain to fail. I remain grateful to him for giving me the resolve to prove the prediction wrong.) Everyone else was pivoting to video. We pivoted to ink and paper, sent via the U.S. Postal Service. Ten years later, we are still here, while a lot of other places that began with a lot more money have folded (see, e.g., the Messenger, which burned through $50 million in a year and then died). The reason we’ve survived is that there are still many people who don’t like that all media is now just transient images on a social media feed. They experience a thrill when they get a cool thing in the mail that they can unwrap and hold. They know that seeing a beautiful illustration on the printed page is different, and better, from seeing it as a JPEG on your phone.
So we don’t really give a damn what the trends in the industry are. We located ourselves in New Orleans when everyone else is in New York. We defiantly publish on obscure topics that aren’t anywhere in the news cycle. (Have you read Alice Millar-Thompson’s article on eel smuggling?) And we’re going to keep paying human artists to create elaborate, gorgeous works of handmade art that take ages to make.
So our rule is simple: No AI generated articles or illustrations in the magazine! We are not going to feed you slop. And we think you should not give money to any publication that does feed you slop, because they’re both treating their audience with contempt, and avoiding paying workers so that their owners can get richer.
This doesn’t mean nobody doing work here can ever use any of the softwares that are broadly lumped together as AI. Much as we respect the Luddites around here, we’re not against technological innovation. Nothing in our rules prohibits writers from using a new tool to help them research something, or prevents an artist from using a tool to, say, add a texture or change a color, or make some kind of small element. But we need, first, to ensure that technologies are a tool used by workers to help them, rather than a tool used to replace workers. And, second, we need to make sure that readers aren’t being fed things that look like people’s genuine thoughts and creative expression but are in fact the product of disembodied mathematical formulas.
I’ll admit, I used to be excited by generative AI. I made goofy little images in DALL-E. I liked the dumb novelty songs. I thought it could be a cool tool for creative professionals to play around with. I forgot for a moment that we live under capitalism, where every new technology will be used by the ruling class to fuck over workers. As Garrison Lovely writes in his new book Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion Dollar Race to Replace Us—and How to Stop It, the developers of AI don’t see it as an asset for workers, but as a way to replace them. They’re trying to build a device whose success is literally measured by whether it successfully replaces people. It is not being designed to help the average person’s capacity to achieve their goals, but to help automate us all into obsolescence. That’s why it has to be fought aggressively.
We at Current Affairs are not capitalists. There are no profits to be made here. We’re a unionized 501c3 organization, which means that we have no incentive to try to replace our workers with machines. So we’re going to demonstrate that you don’t have to do this, that there’s another way, and that it results in better media that is more pleasurable to read and more informative. It’s not going to be easy, because competitor publications are going to be able to produce immense quantities of writing in the time we are painstakingly correcting and adjusting a single article.
But like John Henry, before we let that steam drill beat us, we will die with our hammer in our hand.

We need your help to keep putting out this handmade magazine. Subscribe or donate today. Your money pays real writers and real artists to make the world’s most beautiful printed publication. If you value authentic human thought and culture, get Current Affairs today.

articles.sourceTitle: Apple ML Research: Muse Spark Open with MLX on Mac Studio
articles.title: Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio
articles.text:
content type Featured highlightLocal and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac StudioMLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post, we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.
In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1), well above average human reading speed.
Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio.
Muse Spark Open Decode SpeedContext size of 8,192 tokensFigure 1: Muse Spark Open decode speed in tokens per second, on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, at a context size of 8,192 tokens. Higher is better. We report performance for three parallelization schemes: pipeline parallelization over two Mac Studio computers (2 M5 Pipeline), and tensor parallelization over two (2 M5 Tensor) and four Mac Studio (4 M5 Tensor) computers.

We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio, using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post. We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads.
We evaluate three frontier-class models (Table 1) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts — and thus parameters — active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).
ModelTotal ParametersActive ParametersNative PrecisionEvaluation PrecisionMuse Spark Open816B42BBF16NVFP4Mistral Medium 3.5128B128BFP8FP8Qwen 3.827B27BBF16BF16Table 1: Language models used in this post. Models ship in various precision formats; we evaluate Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 in their native precision, and Muse Spark Open in 4-bit (NVFP4) precision.
Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark. For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line:
mlx_lm.benchmark --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1

A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes.
Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3, respectively.

Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In Figure 2, we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra.
Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6× faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see Figure 2). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts.
Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see Figure 3), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6× faster tokens/s.
TTFT SpeedupSingle Mac Studio, M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline (1.0×)Figure 2: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup on M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. The M5 Ultra GPU Neural Accelerator shines on compute-bound workloads.
Decode SpeedupSingle Mac Studio, M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline (1.0×)Figure 3: Decode speedup on M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Decode is memory-bandwidth bound, and the M5 Ultra’s 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth (vs 819 GB/s on the M3 Ultra) is a key advantage.
The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra — a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment.
Peak Power ConsumptionContext size of 65,536 tokensFigure 4: Peak power consumption (in watts) during Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 inference, at a context size of 65,536 tokens, on Mac Studio with M3 Ultra and with M5 Ultra.
While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.

Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the model’s inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the model’s layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes.
Splitting Large Models Across Multiple ComputersFigure 5: MLX supports two approaches to splitting large models across multiple computers. With pipeline parallelization, a model is split across depth, while with tensor parallelization, a model is split across width.
MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation. These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives (jaccl, pronounced “jackal”) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that jaccl uses. Once the hosts are set up, MLX provides mlx.launch, a helper command to launch jobs across multiple nodes:
mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 --prefill-step-size 8192 --pipeline

In this command, --backend jaccl specifies the RDMA Thunderbolt driver backend. The --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 flag enables an experimental MLX feature for fast CPU-GPU synchronization, reducing communication overhead between the CPU (which initiates the Thunderbolt communication) and the GPU (which does the compute).
In general, decode inference speed with pipeline parallelization (see Figure 7) is very similar to that of a single machine, since the layers are still evaluated sequentially. Communication overhead is also very low, as only the intermediate outputs between the two sets of layers need to be exchanged.
It is however notable that for very large contexts (65,536 tokens in our benchmark), pipeline parallelization ends up faster than a single node for prefill — up to ~1.8× faster (see Figure 6). This is because MLX segments large contexts into smaller chunks (here, 8,192 tokens, as set by --prefill-step-size 8192) and pipelines the prefill across the machines: while the second machine computes the later layers of chunk kkk, the first machine computes the earlier layers of chunk k+1k+1k+1, so consecutive chunks overlap in time. For even better compute parallelization, we next turn to tensor parallelization.
TTFT SpeedupTwo Mac Studios with pipeline parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0×)Figure 6: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup of two M5 Ultras with pipeline parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Splitting the context (here into 8,192-token chunks) lets MLX overlap computation across the two machines — hence the speedup at 65,536 but not 8,192.
Decode SpeedupTwo Mac Studios with pipeline parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0×)Figure 7: Decode speedup of two M5 Ultras with pipeline parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Pipeline parallelization leaves decode speed essentially unchanged.

Tensor parallelization (see Figure 5) distributes the LLM’s width across several computers, in contrast to pipeline parallelization, which distributes the model across its depth. Each machine now holds a fraction of each of the layers of the model, such that per-layer computation is parallelized. When efficiently implemented, tensor parallelization improves inference speed. However, tensor parallelization is more complex to implement than pipeline parallelization: each layer must be parallelized, which increases code complexity. The scheme also involves many small communication operations: for each input token and for each layer, one must broadcast inputs and aggregate outputs. As a result, a very low-latency communication technology like Thunderbolt RDMA, supported by MLX jaccl, is critical for this approach to yield any speedup.
With MLX’s high-level mlx.launch helper, it is easy to switch to tensor parallelization. The Mac Studio computers are connected in a Thunderbolt mesh, with each pair of machines linked peer-to-peer by two Thunderbolt cables. Assuming the hosts are set up, we simply launch the benchmark across multiple machines with:
mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1

Figure 8 and Figure 9 show the speedups obtained with two or four Mac Studio computers with M5 Ultra, relative to a single-machine baseline (or, for Muse Spark Open, the pipeline parallelization baseline). Notably, dense architectures scale better across multiple computers.
With a small number of machines, the communication overhead of tensor parallelization can offset some of its compute benefits at very large contexts, though this applie

articles.sourceTitle: Simons Foundation launches $15M effort to help mathematicians navigate AI era
articles.title: Simons Foundation Launches $15M Effort To Help Mathematicians Navigate AI Era – Simons Foundation
articles.text:
The Simons Foundation today announced a new set of initiatives that will help the mathematics community navigate the rapid rise of artificial intelligence in the field.
Under a partnership, the Simons Foundation, Anthropic and OpenAI will commit $15 million in combined funding and resources. The foundation will manage and award funding, including through an open call for proposals, to support workshops and initiatives that help researchers evaluate recent AI-assisted results, learn and use new tools, share perspectives and shape collective standards for AI use.
“As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes the research landscape, we want to help the mathematical community come together and forge the best path forward,” says Simons Foundation President David Spergel. “Now is the time to look at mathematics as a whole — not as a collection of proofs and theorems, but as a collective understanding driven by human curiosity.”
Anthropic and OpenAI will also provide AI tools and computing resources to researchers supported by the Simons Foundation, extending beyond mathematics to include basic science.
The awards and resources will be community-driven and leverage the foundation’s decades-long dedication to supporting and championing mathematics. The foundation was an early backer of machine learning for science, including funding the development of the Lean proof assistant, which has revolutionized how mathematicians work and made AI-assisted proofs possible. Additionally, the foundation has convened workshops, lectures and collaborations that have brought mathematicians together to explore and discuss AI’s role in the field.
“This is a moment for the mathematics community to come together,” Spergel says. “The community should be driving discussions of how these tools are evaluated, adopted and used, not any single company or institution. The goal of the program is to support the mathematics community.”

articles.sourceTitle: Using AI to reverse engineer hardware
articles.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to reverse engineer hardware
articles.text:
After my mother passed away I ended up with a big box full of old film negatives containing photos from childhood family trips and similar. So I decided to buy a negative photo scanner and found that the Plustek 8200i was supported under Linux so I bought that. Only to discover that the chipset in the scanner had changed to one that wasn’t supported under Linux anymore. So I had some success making Linux configuration tools for some of my hardware using Claude code, like my Dell Camera controller app so I thought, maybe Claude can help me get a working SANE driver. I basically got stuck and got nowhere for the longest time and even basically gave up on the project for a few Months.
Then I saw a post on X from Tom Crider aka Glorious Eggroll talking about how he had managed to fix a mouse driver using AI tooling. He basically described how he set it up so that the AI agent had full control of a Windows instance to capture data needed to fix the driver. So I pasted his tweet into Claude and asked it to help me set up a windows virtual machine to do the same things Tom as doing for my scanner. I think the combination of having the ability to run scans under windows and capture the USB data while doing so worked wonders, probably combined with improvements to Claude code made a huge difference. Within a few hours I had my first ever working scan under Linux, sure with some quality issues, but 100% recognizable as the image in the negative. Some days later I had a near perfect driver, including support for Infrared scanning ready to go, only to discover that in the time between me giving up and then trying again someone had committed code to SANE to support the scanner already…..it happens sometimes. I also used Claude to write an application for doing negative scanning, which I named Negative Vibes, thought that was a cute name.
Anyway, with the success of my scanner effort I thought, I wonder if I can use this to finally fix the last issues with MIPI camera support on my laptop. So I told claude to re-use the harness I had created and try to fix the MIPI camera on my laptop by updating the kernel driver and libcamera as needed. I started the job in the morning and by the end of the day I had a much improved situation with patches for both the kernel and libcamera ready.
So I thought that this might be worthwhile sharing with the world, and while anyone could start from scratch I did ask Claude to make the harness generic and document it to make the pathway for anyone else who wants to try this on their hardware a little easier. Writing a driver for undocumented hardware has always been tedious. You capture bus traffic, stare at hex dumps, and form hypotheses about what each register or control transfer does. You then test them one at a time, usually for weeks. None of it is conceptually hard, but it takes a lot of patience and skills.
That kind of work suits an AI model well. It can read thousands of lines of USB capture, notice that a sequence repeats with one byte changing, and propose what that byte means. It can write the test to confirm it, and it doesn’t get bored. The human still decides what to build and checks that it works on real hardware, but the slog shrinks a lot.
hw-harness
Be aware that I did not use hw-harness in this form for my projects as this was basically bespoke code at that time, so this project is an attempt to make the harness more generic and shareable from the scripts I was using while doing the work. What hw-harness is meant to help your Claude or Codex session with:
1. Record a reference session. Run the vendor’s Windows driver in a KVM virtual machine, with the real device passed through to the guest.

2. Capture from outside the VM. Record the traffic on the Linux host with usbmon. It sits below the passthrough layer, so the guest can’t see it.

3. Repeat the same operation on Linux with your own driver, and capture that the same way.

4. Diff the two traces. Both come from the same instrument, so they compare directly. The differences are your list of driver bugs.
For devices with no bus to tap, such as an internal MIPI camera, the harness uses Windows-side inspection instead. That means INF files, registry data, ACPI tables and device properties.
The approach should be fine in the sense it doesn’t rely on copying any code instead it observes what the hardware does and only extract configuration data from the Windows drivers, so every constant in the new driver traces back to something recorded.
So for those interested I have 3 short descriptions of the projects I did and what was needed.
Project 1: a SANE backend for the Plustek OpticFilm 8200i

Comparing the driver output of two drivers available. The first project is a SANE backend for the newer Plustek OpticFilm 8200i. It uses the Genesys GL128 controller (USB 07b3:1825) and had no Linux support. The older model with the same name uses a GL845 and is already handled by SANE.
The backend supports:

Color, gray, infrared and color+infrared modes
Resolutions from 300 to 7200 dpi, at 8 or 16 bits per channel
Dust and scratch removal from the infrared channel
An exposure multiplier for dense negatives

It’s packaged as a Fedora RPM, built automatically on every push. I mostly tested it with my own Negative Vibes application as there are not that many options under Linux for negative scanning.
Upstream SANE’s genesys backend also gained support for this scanner in September 2026, so I compared the two. Both resolve the same fine detail at 3600 dpi. Mine is faster at full resolution (34.6 s against 54.4 s) and supports infrared dust removal. Upstream offers more resolution steps. The webpage has an interactive side-by-side comparison you can check out. These are single-unit, single-frame results, so treat them as one data point. Check out the interactive page I made showing the current state of the two drivers, hopefully the discoveries I made can be used by the SANE project to fix some smaller items in the upstream driver. Anyway, I put this project up more as a proof of concept due to that since I expect everyone including myself will use the upstream driver once it reaches parity with this one.
Project 2: Negative Vibes

Full scan of negative completed including infrared cleaning of image. A driver alone isn’t much use if scanning negatives is still painful, so I built Negative Vibes. It’s a GNOME app, written in Rust, for scanning colour and black-and-white negatives and slides on any film-capable SANE scanner.
The scan is kept exactly as the scanner delivered it: 16-bit, linear, with the infrared plane. Everything else is a stack of non-destructive settings on top, so you can change the look and export again. It includes:

Density-space negative inversion with film base and dye-crosstalk correction
Roll-wide settings with per-frame overrides
Infrared and software dust removal
IT8 calibration through ArgyllCMS
Export to TIFF, JPEG, PNG and DNG, with ICC profiles and metadata

It ships as a Flatpak that includes the scanner backend. It’s tested on the 8200i so far. The goal is to support any film scanner SANE supports. For that, SANE needs a standard way to expose infrared channels, which it doesn’t have yet.
Project 3: Fixing the MIPI camera on my ThinkPad
Showing MIPI output before and after fixes. Colors are better than they look as I was sitting in a relatively dark room by the end of the session. The camera in my Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 14 (Aura Edition) uses a Sony IMX471 sensor behind an Intel IPU7. On Linux it produced dark images with heavy vignetting and a strong yellow-green cast. mipi-fixes-x1-aura collects the fixes. It’s only relevant to this laptop, which is why it isn’t one of the bigger packaged projects, but I have already submitted the kernel patches to Kate Hsuan and the libcamera patches is being reviewed by Wim Taymans for submission to Libcamera.
Kernel (IMX471 driver):

A crop-selection bug returned an error before storing the crop rectangle, so libcamera assumed the full pixel array.
The test-pattern register was declared with the wrong width.
The analogue gain cap was too low, which cost about 1.8 stops of sensitivity.

libcamera software ISP:

Lens shading correction was missing entirely, leaving the corners about 2.7 stops darker.
White-balance statistics were summed at the sensor’s native bit depth against an 8-bit black level. That skewed white balance, and the fix applies to any RAW10/RAW12 sensor.

In a controlled low-light test, frame brightness rose from 31.1 to 90.9. The red/green and blue/green ratios moved from 0.890 and 0.672 to 1.047 and 0.823, close to a USB webcam reference. Blue is still about 17% short in low light, which I put down to grey-world white balance. Fedora 44 RPMs are on the releases page.
What I learned

Reference captures are a big step. Having the AI compare a known-good trace against a failing one turns a vague “it doesn’t work” into a concrete list of differences. For example for the MIPI camera having a USB camera also connected so Claude could compare the two captures was critical.
The AI is good at the tedium. That covers decoding captures, writing probes and cross-checking constants. I still have to be the one holding the physical hardware.
Real hardware is the only judge. Every claim above was checked on the actual scanner or laptop.

If you have hardware with no Linux driver, try hw-harness. Thanks again to Glorious Eggroll for the inspiration.
NOTE: I am not claiming that my scans or MIPI camera is perfect now, but the scanner gives me decent looking scans and the MIPI camera looks a lot better than before. So over time I am sure we be able to tweak and polish further, but I am happy that it allowed me to move the needle despite lacking the in-depth knowledge for this type of work.
—

articles.sourceTitle: Show HN: Gemini 4 Argon plays StarCraft
articles.title: StarSkirmish Bench v0.2
articles.text:
TL;DR

StarSkirmish is a benchmark where LLMs write bots for StarCraft: Brood War
Each LLM gets one hour to write a Protoss bot in C++, which is then evaluated against other LLMs' bots and established human written bots
StarSkirmish tests long horizon reasoning and agentic coding as LLMs must incorporate learnings from practice games to improve their StarCraft bot

StarSkirmish Bench v0.2

The StarSkirmish Bench evaluates how strong of a StarCraft bot can each LLM write given 1 hour of wall clock time. v0.2 updates StarSkirmish Bench v0.1 with flagship models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, each running in its lab's 1st party CLI harness.

An LLM’s score reflects its win rate against a roster of competitive human written bots and demo bots.

StarSkirmish Bench v0.2
1 hour runs, in its 1st party CLI harness. Scores are average win rates (0–100) of each model's 5 runs against a roster of competitive human written bots.

Gemini 4 Argon runs at high, the highest reasoning effort available to it; every other model runs at max.

Implementation Details

Objective

Each LLM writes a Protoss bot in C++ against
BWAPI 4.4.0, played on
OpenBW. Games are Protoss versus Protoss on three
ladder maps: Heartbreak Ridge, Benzene and Destination. A game ends when one side's buildings
are all destroyed. Games that reach the 60 minute cap (86,400 frames) are decided as on the
BASIL ladder: the higher kills + razings score wins.

The LLM starts from a skeleton bot that only mines, with the source code of the three demo bots and two standard bot libraries: FAP, a combat simulator, and BWEM, a map analyzer. Whatever is in its bot folder when the hour ends is its final bot, so it has to keep the bot compiling.

The LLM has tools to compile its bot, play practice games, and read each game's summary, transcript and its bot's own log. Practice opponents are grouped into tiers: D (the three demo bots), C and B (three mid-ranked
human written bots each), A (BananaBrain, Locutus) and S (Stardust, PurpleWave).

Every v0.2 harness compacts the model's context at about 250k tokens. When a conversation nears that point, the CLI condenses it and the model carries on. Codex, OpenAI's CLI, for example, gives the GPT models its default 272k token window and triggers compression once 90% filled.

The CLIs' web search and web fetch tools are turned off, and the agent has no other internet access. The CLI is installed before the clock starts, and the hour counts from when the agent starts. There is no submit tool: the harness collects the bot when the time runs out.

Scoring

v0.2 replaces v0.1's Elo ratings with plain win rates. A bot's score is its win rate over its  tournament games, and a model's StarSkirmish Bench score is the average of its 5 bots' scores, from 0 (every game lost) to 100 (every game won).

Because every bot plays the same fixed roster, its games don't depend on the other LLM bots in the field. They all run in parallel, and a new model's bots can be scored without replaying anyone else's. A fixed roster also keeps the bar the same over time, so scores from different model generations are more directly comparable than Elo ratings fitted within one field.

Benchmark Correlations

StarSkirmish no longer tracks the most widely reported evals. It barely moves with the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (ρ 0.26), where GPT-6 Astra, the top model here, only ties for 4th of these 9 models. It has also drifted away from Terminal-Bench 4.0, which it tracked closely in v0.1. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full both rank near the top of Terminal-Bench 4.0 but near the bottom here.

Benchmark Correlation
Each model's StarSkirmish Bench score against its Vals IOI and WeirdML v3 scores, with the Spearman ρ between them. The dashed line is the best straight-line fit.

WeirdML v3 scores 7 of the 9 models: Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder Full have not been included at time of writing.

StarSkirmish still tracks Vals IOI, olympiad programming problems solved in C++, and WeirdML, an independent benchmark of unusual machine learning coding tasks. One reading is that the most heavily benchmarked evals have become targets that models are tuned for, while less targeted tests of long horizon, difficult coding tasks still move together.
